newsitem.title: USA: Wasteful fishing sharply depletes shark populations.
newsitem.headline: Wasteful fishing sharply depletes shark populations.

text.p: With up to 70 million sharks killed annually for a growing trade in their fins and other products, shark populations around the world may plummet and irreversibly change marine ecosystems, the World Wildlife Fund said on Wednesday.
"Sharks are the top ocean predator and we have no idea if we're past the point of no return for some species," Andrea Gaski, author of the WWF report, said in a statement.
"As sharks decline, the balance of their marine ecosystems may be irreversibly affected and impact other important fish populations in those same areas," Gaski said.
The report said unmanaged and wasteful shark catches of 30 million to 70 million annually may cause commercial fisheries to collapse, eliminate species in some areas and deplete migratory stocks.

"Unless action is taken by national and international fisheries agencies, many shark fisheries, which have become economic alternatives to other crashing fisheries throughout the world, will rapidly share the same fate," according to the report by the WWF's trade monitoring programme called TRAFFIC.

A three-year research effort found expanded trade and increased availability around the world of shark products including fins, meat, livers and other parts for food or use in health and beauty treatments, the report said.

Fins used in Asian cuisine are the world's most expensive fisheries product, the report said, and are so desirable that in some cases sharks' fins are cut off and the fish is dumped back in the water, sometimes still alive.
The deadly predators, which inhabit all of the world's oceans, are particularly vulnerable to overfishing because they have long life cycles and reproduce slowly.

More than 19 countries and territories report annual catches of 10,000 metric tons or more, with the world's total catch reported at more than 730,000 tons in 1994 and at least another 250,000 tons discarded as bycatch, the report said.
Indonesia catches the most sharks, and has more than doubled its catch from 42,900 metric tons in 1980 to 92,900 in 1994, the report said.
